core: What a philosophy of education is: a normative set of commitments about aims, worthwhile knowledge, and the roles of teacher and learner
The four philosophical roots usually taught first: idealism, realism, pragmatism, existentialism
Perennialism: enduring truths, liberal arts, cultivation of intellect; Hutchins and Adler
Essentialism: a defined common core of skills and shared knowledge, teacher authority; Bagley and Hirsch
Progressivism: experience, inquiry, integrated and problem-based curriculum; Dewey and pragmatism
Social reconstructionism and its descendant critical pedagogy: schooling aimed at social reform; Counts, Brameld, Freire
Existentialism in education: individual choice, responsibility, meaning-making; Morris and Maxine Greene
Three diagnostic questions used to compare the positions: what is worth knowing, what is the teacher's role, how should learning be organized
The epistemic status of the taxonomy: analytic frameworks for examining beliefs, not empirically validated categories, and teachers commonly blend them
Why essentialism and perennialism are easily confused, and what actually separates them
supporting: Teacher-centered versus student-centered as a tendency rather than a rule (perennialist Socratic seminar as the counterexample)
The religious (Aquinas, Maritain) and secular (Hutchins, Adler) strands within perennialism
Freire's conscientizacao / critical consciousness and the critique of 'banking' education
The Eurocentric selection of the canonical philosophies taught in U.S. teacher preparation
'Progressive' in education names Dewey's tradition, not a contemporary partisan label
outOfScope: Behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, and social learning theory (separate topics in the Learning Theories unit)
History of U.S. public education as an institution (separate topic in this unit)
Postmodernism, critical race theory, and other later positions covered in advanced foundations courses
Lesson planning, instructional strategies, and assessment design (later units)
Advice on how any individual teacher, school, or district should set policy

claims.claim: Teacher-preparation texts commonly present perennialism, essentialism, progressivism, and social reconstructionism (often with existentialism) as the major philosophies of education, and organize them around what should be taught and how.

Idealism, realism, pragmatism, and existentialism are the four philosophical schools normally taught as the roots of educational philosophies; idealism and realism trace to Plato and Aristotle, while pragmatism (Peirce, James, Dewey) and existentialism (Kierkegaard, Nietzsche) are more recent.
Perennialism holds that some truths and works have enduring importance across time and place, favors a liberal-arts curriculum taken by all students, and aims at cultivating the intellect.

Robert Maynard Hutchins led the University of Chicago from 1929 to 1951, championed a general-education college curriculum and the 'great books', and co-taught great-books courses with Mortimer Adler; the university never formally adopted the great books program into its curriculum.
Mortimer Adler argued for a single course of study appropriate for all students and opposed separate vocational, technical, and academic tracks; his Paideia Proposal was issued in 1982.

Essentialism, associated with William C. Bagley's 1938 'An Essentialist's Platform for the Advancement of American Education', argues for a strong common core curriculum, high standards, and a well-prepared teacher as the classroom authority; E. D. Hirsch Jr.'s Cultural Literacy (1987) and the Core Knowledge Foundation continue the tradition.

Perennialism and essentialism are easily confused because both are content-first and largely teacher-centered; they differ in what justifies the content. Perennialism holds that the truths it teaches do not change and aims at individual intellectual development, while essentialism selects a core of skills and shared knowledge on the grounds of what students need to be competent, productive members of society now.

Progressivism rests on pragmatism, treats learning as experiential and problem-centered, integrates curriculum across subjects, and gives students shared authority in planning; John Dewey is its central figure.

Dewey founded and directed a laboratory school at the University of Chicago (1896-1904; Dewey joined the faculty in 1894) and published Democracy and Education in 1916, where he defines education as the reconstruction or reorganization of experience that adds to the meaning of experience and increases the ability to direct later experience.

Democracy and Education repeatedly attacks dualisms in educational theory (mind and body, method and subject matter, individual and world), so a strict either-or between child-centered and subject-centered teaching misrepresents Dewey's own position.

Social reconstructionism emerged from progressive educators in the 1920s and 1930s who held that schools should actively work to build a more equitable social order; George S. Counts addressed the Progressive Education Association in 1932 in the talks published as Dare the School Build a New Social Order?, and Theodore Brameld is regarded as a founder of the position.

Paulo Freire, whose Pedagogy of the Oppressed was first published in Portuguese in 1968, belongs to the social reconstructionist and critical pedagogy lineage; he criticised the 'banking' model in which students are treated as vessels to be filled, favoured problem-posing education, and aimed at conscientizacao, or critical consciousness, on the view that knowledge and language are never neutral.

In an existentialist classroom, subject matter is secondary to the student's self-understanding, the teacher's job is to create conditions for free choice and personal responsibility, and standardized measurement is strongly opposed.

Maxine Greene (1917-2014), a philosopher of education at Teachers College, Columbia University, identified as an existentialist, drew on Sartre, Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty, and argued for 'wide-awakeness', imagination, freedom, and aesthetic education.

Presenting philosophy of education as a set of competing orientations is only one of several ways the field has been organized; other overviews group work by the philosophical subfield it draws on or by topic, and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's own overview uses a topical organization.
The teacher-centered / student-centered contrast is a tendency rather than a rule: perennialist classrooms are largely teacher-centered yet use student-centered activities such as Socratic seminar.

The philosophies taught as foundational in U.S. teacher preparation are a selection reflecting a narrow, Eurocentric range of perspectives, and exclude educational traditions from many other societies.
Van Cleve Morris's Existentialism in Education: What It Means (Harper & Row, 1966) introduced existentialism as an educational position into American teacher-education literature.

Foundations-of-education texts treat these positions as beliefs a candidate should locate themselves across, using self-assessment and reflection to build a personal philosophy of education, rather than as exclusive types a teacher belongs to.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many 'major philosophies of education' there are, and whether existentialism belongs on the list.
positions: Open Oregon and SUNY Oneonta present four philosophical perspectives (essentialism, perennialism, progressivism, social reconstructionism/critical pedagogy) and treat existentialism only as a general philosophy.

The Kansas State text lists six philosophies of education (perennialism, progressivism, behaviorism, essentialism, social reconstructionism, postmodernism) and treats existentialism as one of four schools of philosophy with educational implications.
Many teacher-preparation courses teach a five-item list that includes existentialism as an educational philosophy in its own right.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the five-item set named in the assignment, states explicitly that lists differ by textbook, and explains that existentialism appears both as a root philosophy and as an educational position. It does not claim a single canonical count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Hutchins should be described as president or chancellor of the University of Chicago.
positions: The University of Chicago Office of the President page is headed 'Robert Maynard Hutchins, 1929-1951'.
The Kansas State text calls him 'a chancellor of the University of Chicago'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says he led the University of Chicago from 1929 to 1951, which both sources support, and avoids the title dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Counts belongs to progressivism or social reconstructionism.
positions: Counts delivered his 1932 challenge to the Progressive Education Association and worked within the progressive movement.
He is standardly named as a founder of the society-centered social reconstructionist position.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson places Counts in social reconstructionism while noting he emerged from and argued with the progressive movement, which is what the sources describe.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive content about educational philosophies at all: it defined the topic only as 'a foundational concept in Education' and offered no philosophies, figures, or distinctions.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined 'Major Philosophies Of Education' circularly as 'a foundational Education concept covered in this lesson'.
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study advice rather than any content in the topic.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with researched content naming the five philosophies, their philosophical roots, and their principal advocates.

Added verified attributions (Hutchins and Adler to perennialism; Bagley and Hirsch to essentialism; Dewey to progressivism; Counts, Brameld and Freire to social reconstructionism; Morris and Greene to existentialism in education) rather than asserting lineages from memory.
Added an explicit statement that these are normative frameworks for examining beliefs, not empirically validated categories, and that teachers blend them.
Excluded behaviorism, cognitivism, and constructivism, which belong to the Learning Theories unit, and added a common mistake warning against confusing progressivism with constructivism.
Added the perennialism-versus-essentialism distinction the assignment flagged as a frequent point of confusion.

Did not repeat the Kansas State chapter's claims that Bagley blamed immigration for weakening American schools, or that 1930s U.S. students were measured against Japanese and German students, since no corroborating source was found.

Softened the perennialism-versus-essentialism contrast: an earlier draft asserted that essentialism's list of essentials is expected to change over time. That specific claim appeared only in a search-engine summary of an OER chapter that could not be retrieved and verified directly, so the distinction was rewritten to rest on what justifies the content, which the verified sources do support.

Replaced an unsourced empirical assertion that 'most teachers blend the philosophies' with the supported observation that foundations texts ask candidates to locate their beliefs across the positions via self-assessment and reflection, which is what the Open Oregon chapter actually does.
rightsIssues: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no derivative or adapted text was produced from it, and it is recorded REFERENCE_ONLY.

The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, the University of Chicago president's office page, and the Teachers College memorial article are all-rights-reserved; facts were synthesized and all wording is original. Recorded REFERENCE_ONLY.
The one direct quotation in the lesson is from Dewey's Democracy and Education (1916), which Project Gutenberg records as public domain in the USA.

Open Oregon (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and SUNY Oneonta via Lumen (CC BY) permit reuse with attribution, and the Kansas State text is dedicated to the public domain; even so, no source prose was copied or paraphrase-followed.
